transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—I'm Dr. [Name]. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, Doctor. Um… I guess what brings me in is that I’ve been feeling like I’m always kind of moving from one thing to the next. Like I don’t really idle very well, if that makes sense. I’ve managed it okay for a long time, or at least I think I have, but with the new setup at work it’s been harder to sort of keep it from showing. I’m not trying to make it sound worse than it is, but it’s been bothering me enough that I thought I should ask about it.
Can you tell me whether you noticed this same kind of restlessness or trouble slowing down back when you were a child, or is this something that's really only become noticeable as an adult?

I think it was there when I was a kid, yeah. I don’t want to overstate it, but looking back it wasn’t just this job change.

In grade school, teachers would write things like I was bright, but careless, or that I talked out of turn. And I remember getting reminded to stay with my work. At the time it was kind of brushed off as just me being… I don’t know, energetic or not careful enough. But yes, it does seem like some version of this was around back then too.
Do you often find yourself acting or speaking impulsively—like interrupting people, blurting out answers, or making quick decisions without thinking them through—in your day-to-day life now?

Yeah… I mean, I try not to. I really don’t want to come across as rude or like I think I know better than people.

But at work, if I hear a coworker talking through a customer issue, sometimes I’ll jump in with the answer before they’ve finished explaining it, or before they’ve actually asked me. In my head I’m trying to be helpful, but I can see how it might feel like I’m interrupting. I do catch myself afterward and think, “Okay, maybe I should’ve waited.”
Do you often feel physically restless—like needing to fidget, get up and move around, or feeling like you can't sit still for long periods, especially in situations like meetings or long tasks?

Yeah, I do, somewhat. I mean, I can sit through things if I have to, so I don’t want to make it sound like I’m jumping out of my chair all the time.

But if it’s something like a training video or a slow appointment, I start feeling kind of boxed in. Like I really want to stand up, stretch, shift around, or at least have something to do with my hands. I try to keep it subtle, you know, so it’s not distracting to anyone.
Would you say these patterns—jumping in, restlessness, trouble focusing—cause noticeable problems not just at work, but also in other areas of your life, like at home or in your relationships?

I’d say it’s most noticeable at work, to be honest. I don’t want to make it sound like I’m falling apart or anything, because I do try hard and I think I get along pretty well with customers.

But it has started coming up in my reviews. My supervisors have pointed out unfinished tickets, or mistakes that end up slowing the team down. That’s hard to hear, because I’m not trying to be careless. I guess that’s probably the clearest place where it’s causing actual problems.
Can you give me a specific example of a time these patterns—like losing focus, jumping in, or restlessness—caused a problem at home or in a relationship, rather than at work?

Yeah… I guess at home it shows up more in small ways, not huge arguments or anything.

Like if my wife and I are watching a movie, especially something slower, I’ll start shifting around or making little comments, or I’ll get up to check something in the kitchen or do some small thing. I don’t mean to ruin it for her, but I know it can probably be annoying when she’s just trying to relax and watch.

Same with reading at home. I’ll sit down thinking, “Okay, I’m going to relax,” and then before long I’m moving around or finding a reason to get up. It’s not terrible, but… yeah, I can see how it affects the quiet time we’re supposed to be having together.
Do you often find it hard to stay focused on tasks or conversations—like losing track of what you're doing, or having your mind wander—even when you're trying to pay attention?

Yeah, I think so… not constantly, but enough that I notice it.

Like in the longer coaching meetings, or if I’m reading through a new procedure, I’ll start out trying to pay attention and I feel like I’m following it. Then a few minutes later I realize my eyes have been moving along, or I’ve been sitting there listening, but I didn’t really absorb what was said.

It’s a little embarrassing, because I’m not trying to ignore anyone. I just kind of lose the thread and then have to catch myself up. Does that make sense?
Thinking back to before you turned 12 years old, can you recall specific examples—like trouble finishing schoolwork, fidgeting in class, or blurting out answers—that were noticeable at that age?

Yeah… I mean, looking back, I guess it probably was there pretty early. I don’t want to overstate it, because I did okay in school overall, but I remember teachers saying things like I was bright but careless.

On report cards or comments, there’d be stuff about me talking out of turn, or needing reminders to stay with my work. I think that was grade school, before middle school. At the time it just felt like normal kid stuff, but… looking back, it does sound like some of the same pattern, I guess.

latest_inference.note: Patient confirms childhood onset (before age 12) with documented inattentive and impulsive symptoms (careless, talking out of turn, needing reminders), current impairment across work and home settings, and presence of both inattentive (losing focus, mind wandering) and hyperactive-impulsive (restlessness, interrupting, blurting) symptoms. This supports combined presentation ADHD, meeting core diagnostic criteria including cross-situational impairment and childhood onset.
